textContent.text: Surfing tends to conjure up images of bathing suits, balmy breezes, and the warm waves of Hawaii or Costa Rica—but surfing conditions aren't always so pleasant. The waters off the coast of Northern California, for example, are uncomfortably cold year-round, and even in Australia, surfers need something to keep them warm in cooler months. For generations, wetsuits have allowed surfers, swimmers, and divers to enjoy bodies of water across the globe and in every season. Wetsuits insulate users, protecting them from both dangerously cold temperatures and ocean threats like rocky reefs and jellyfish stings. Some wetsuits can even reduce the severity of shark bites.

The invention of the modern wetsuit is now generally credited to Hugh Bradner, a physicist at the University of California, Berkeley. In 1951, Bradner spearheaded a project to protect U.S. Navy divers from hypothermia, a condition that occurs when a person's body temperature drops dangerously low. He correctly theorized that a wetsuit with insulating materials did not have to keep a person dry to provide warmth. If a thin layer of water became trapped between the body and the suit, it would quickly warm to body temperature. Bradner experimented with tight-fitting neoprene, a type of synthetic rubber that proved to be effective as insulation.

Bradner himself was not successful in selling his wetsuit in the consumer market, but competitors quickly embraced the use of neoprene. In San Francisco, former naval pilot Jack O'Neill opened one of the world's first surf shops in 1952 and sold neoprene wetsuits to his fellow surfers. Eventually, the business that O'Neill originally launched from his garage expanded into an international company. Along the way, he made changes to Bradner's design, experimenting with different seams, zippers, and a variety of styles. O'Neill's early suits had names like "The Shorty," "The Long John," and "The Beaver Tail Jacket."

Around the same time as O'Neill entered the wetsuit market, farther south in Manhattan Beach, California, twins Bob and Bill Meistrell started a surf-wear company called Body Glove. Legend has it that the company name was inspired by Bill saying his wetsuits "fit like a glove." Like O'Neill and Bradner, the Meistrells made suits out of neoprene. Competing assertions were made over the years about the true inventor of the neoprene wetsuit, with many insisting that it was O'Neill or the Meistrells. But by the early twenty-first century, the original breakthrough was finally attributed to Bradner.

Despite their effectiveness, the Bradner, O'Neill, and Body Glove wetsuits of the 1950s were far from perfect. Early suits were stiff and difficult to get on and off; surfers often used talcum powder to help the rubbery material move more smoothly over their skin. Moreover, these wetsuits were easily torn, stretched, and otherwise damaged. Soon, a rising interest in surfing and other ocean sports would increase the demand for better wetsuit performance.

The 1960s saw a surfing boom, with young people up and down the coastlines of the world taking up the sport. Thanks to Bradner's discovery and the commercial innovations of O'Neill and the Meistrell twins, wetsuits evolved into a surfing essential. As the sport grew in popularity, manufacturers continued to improve wetsuit technology, experimenting with multiple layers, alternative stitching techniques, and new materials, such as nylon. These updates led to the flexible, comfortable, and durable wetsuits that surfers and other aquatic athletes rely on today.

Bradner experimented with tight-fitting neoprene, a type of synthetic rubber that proved to be effective as insulation.

Bradner himself was not successful in selling his wetsuit in the consumer market, but competitors quickly embraced the use of neoprene. textContent.text: For many people around the world, wheelchairs are a key to mobility and independence. These incredible devices are so important that it's hard to imagine a time when they didn't exist. Although nobody knows exactly when the first wheelchair was invented, historical records show that people have been experimenting with this form of transportation for many centuries.

A medical illustration from the 1590s shows an early version of the wheelchair used by King Philip II of Spain, who lost his mobility due to painful joint diseases. His wheelchair was upholstered and propped on four wheels, with leg rests and an adjustable back. It was most likely pushed with the help of an attendant. In 1655, a German watchmaker named Stephan Farfler, who didn't have use of his legs, designed a three-wheeled model that resembled a large tricycle. The device was made of wood and was exceptionally heavy, but it had an innovative feature: The forward wheel was controlled by a hand crank, allowing users to propel the vehicle without assistance. Farfler's invention is considered by many to be the first self-driven wheelchair.

Wheelchairs became increasingly common in the late 1800s and early 1900s, with catalogs for surgical and medical equipment featuring different types of designs. Some of these wheelchairs had rubber tires, as well as circular hand rims attached to the wheels that users rotated to propel themselves. Yet despite these helpful features, most wheelchairs of the time remained cumbersome and difficult to transport. Many were heavy and unwieldy devices made of wood, cane, wicker, or iron.

This changed in 1932, when mining engineer Herbert A. Everest and mechanical engineer Harry C. Jennings introduced a folding wheelchair made of steel. This lighter, more portable design meant users could pack their wheelchairs away for easy transportation. This folding wheelchair soon became the industry standard, and Everest & Jennings, Inc. dominated the market for some time. Then, in the 1950s, Canadian inventor George Klein developed the world's first practical electric wheelchair; his goal was to help paralyzed World War II veterans who couldn't push a manual wheelchair on their own. Everest & Jennings marketed Klein's invention to a broad audience, securing the company's reputation as a vanguard of wheelchair technology.

Wheelchair design continued to advance through the late twentieth century, and it is still evolving today. Modern wheelchairs are lighter, and padded seats and armrests make them more comfortable than ever. Many are designed to accommodate users' particular needs and body measurements, with some having the ability to recline. There are waterproof wheelchairs made for showering and narrow wheelchairs that allow for easier airplane travel. All-terrain wheelchairs transport users over gravel, dirt, and sand. Some wheelchairs are even designed for specific sports, including basketball, tennis, and racing. Having come so far—and with so many unique designs to choose from—the modern wheelchair continues to provide practical mobility solutions for a wide range of users.

pieces.text: Every day, over one hundred million people around the world choose to wear contact lenses. Called "contacts" for short, these lenses correct people's vision just like glasses do. But unlike glasses, contacts are placed directly on the

—the clear, dome-shaped layer that sits over the pupil of the eye. Some people prefer contacts due to the wider field of vision they offer, while others enjoy how small and lightweight they are. Active people like athletes and dancers often wear contacts because they stay in place, even during vigorous movement.

textContent.text: The contacts that people wear today are thin, soft, and fit comfortably on the eye. But it wasn't always that way. The earliest contact lenses were invented in the late 1800s by a German ophthalmologist, or eye doctor, named Adolf Fick. Fick's lenses were hard glass discs that fit across the entire eye—including the white parts! Although these contacts did improve vision a little, they could only be worn for a few hours at a time because they were extremely uncomfortable. Not long after, another German inventor named August Müller created similar glass "cornea-lenses" in the hope of correcting his vision. While his myopia, or nearsightedness, improved, Müller's contacts were also painful to wear and had to be removed frequently. The technology was promising, but contacts were still far from perfect.

pieces.text: In the late 1930s, a plastic called

replaced glass as the preferred material for contacts. This new type of plastic was light, durable, and scratch-resistant. Another major breakthrough came—by accident—in 1948. Stories differ, but according to one version of events, optical technician Kevin Tuohy was shaping a lens when he unintentionally removed its outer edge. His lens still covered the cornea but left the white of the eye uncovered. Tuohy tried the lens on and found that it stayed in place, even when he blinked. In addition to its smaller size, this new design encouraged better eye health by allowing tears to move more freely behind the lens.

textContent.text: Although these innovations marked significant progress, a major problem still remained; like glass lenses before them, polymethyl methacrylate lenses did not allow oxygen to permeate their surface. While most tissues in the body receive oxygen from red blood cells, the cornea receives its supply from the atmosphere. By depriving the eye of oxygen, these contacts caused the cornea to swell. This challenge was eventually solved in the 1970s with the invention of breathable plastics. These materials allowed oxygen to reach the cornea, paving the way for today's safer and more comfortable lenses. Modern lenses can be worn for extended periods, with some designed for continuous use even over several weeks. They are also affordable and disposable, helping millions of people see better with no discomfort and little risk.

textContent.text: During World War II, as American men left their jobs to fight abroad, the country faced a significant labor shortage. This gap in the workforce created new opportunities for women to step into roles and professions that had traditionally been reserved for men. One remarkable woman who seized this opportunity was Mary Golda Ross, a pioneering engineer of Cherokee descent who made significant contributions to top-secret aerospace projects.

Ross was born in 1908 near Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the capital of the Cherokee Nation. At a young age, she developed an interest in math, science, and astronomy, later graduating from Northeastern State Teachers College with a degree in mathematics. Ross became a math and science teacher, and she continued to pursue her graduate studies during her summer breaks. In 1930, she earned her master's degree in mathematics from Colorado State Teachers College. After the United States got involved in World War II, many mathematicians working on military technology were sent overseas to fight, leaving their positions empty. As a result, Ross found work as a mathematical research assistant at Lockheed Aircraft Corporation in Burbank, California.

At Lockheed, Ross joined thirty-nine other engineers as a founding member of a secret think tank known as Skunk Works; at the time, she was the only woman on the team besides the secretary. This team was tasked with improving the designs of American military planes, including the P-38 Lightning. The P-38, one of the most powerful single-seat, twin-engine fighter planes at the time, could climb 3,300 feet in one minute and travel at speeds of up to 400 mph. One of Ross's roles was to recommend changes to the plane's shape and structure to provide greater stability at high speeds.

In 1945, when the war was over and men began returning home, many women were forced out of their jobs—but Ross was not one of them. Not only did Lockheed keep her on staff, but the company sent her to the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), where she became the first Native American woman to earn a professional certification in engineering. At UCLA, Ross studied aeronautics (the science of flight) and celestial mechanics (the movement of objects in space), preparing her for the next phase of an already remarkable career.

Two years after the end of World War II, the Cold War began. Lasting until 1991, the Cold War was an extended period of political strife and intense competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. During this time, Lockheed created a division called the Lockheed Missiles and Space Company, where Ross and her team worked on a number of endeavors, including projects for the military. She played a key role, for instance, in designing Polaris, America's first submarine-launched ballistic missile. She was also involved in the design of the Agena rocket, which was created to carry different kinds of cargo into outer space. Many of Ross's contributions were part of top-secret programs and remain classified even today, but it's no secret that she formulated early ideas for interplanetary space travel. In fact, Ross and her colleagues wrote research papers about how we might conduct missions to Mars and Venus.

In 1973, Ross retired from Lockheed and dove into a different type of work supporting and advocating for women and Native people in the field of engineering. She remained committed to this cause for decades until her passing in 2008, just months shy of her one hundredth birthday.

textContent.text: Inventions often begin with a single person attempting to solve a specific problem. For wealthy socialite Josephine Cochran, that problem was chipped heirloom dishes. The Cochrans used valuable, fragile dishes during the parties they hosted at their Ohio home. But this fine china was regularly damaged afterward during handwashing. Determined to find a solution to this problem, Cochran devised an ingenious invention in the late 1800s that eventually transformed the modern American kitchen: the dishwasher.

Cochran's great-grandfather had been an inventor, and her father was a civil engineer, but Cochran herself received no formal scientific or mechanical training. Still, working in the shed behind her home, she set out to design a machine for washing dishes. Cochran's dishwasher had various wire compartments individually designed to hold specific types of dishes, including plates, cups, and saucers. The compartments fit inside a wheel, which was laid flat inside a copper boiler that heated water. As a motor turned the wheel, soapy water was pumped from the boiler and distributed evenly across the compartments. To clean the dishes, Cochran's device relied on water pressure instead of potentially harmful scrubbers, so the dishware remained intact. While others had designed similar machines—such as a hand-cranked model patented in 1865 that spun a rack of dishes through water—none were as effective as Cochran's invention.

Just as Cochran was starting work on her design, tragedy struck: her husband William died, and she inherited his debt. Instead of hindering her, this hardship only motivated Cochran, who became more determined than ever to develop a commercially successful dishwasher. Cochran formed a company and patented her design in 1886, naming the machine the Cochran Dishwasher. The next step was to convince people to buy it.

Cochran knew that her most obvious target audience was women, who at that time were largely responsible for domestic tasks. But she also knew it would be difficult to persuade them to buy a device that, while efficient, was costly and not truly essential. Therefore, instead of selling to individual homemakers, Cochran chose to prioritize marketing to restaurants and hotels. In 1887, a friend put Cochran in touch with the manager of Chicago's Palmer House, one of the nation's most well-known hotels. The meeting was a success, and the manager purchased Cochran's first dishwasher. Cochran went on to sell her device to a few individual consumers, but businesses remained her most lucrative customer base by far. Her success was recognized in 1893, when the Cochran Dishwasher was honored at the Chicago World's Fair with an award for design and durability.

Despite the dishwasher's success, early versions of the machine were not without shortcomings. Cochran's dishwasher was too large for the average residential kitchen and required more hot water than most homes could produce. Moreover, soapy residue made the dishes seem only partially clean. Many of these issues were later put to rest by the manufacturer of KitchenAid appliances, the company that acquired Cochran's business shortly after her death in 1913.

In 1949, the first KitchenAid in-home dishwasher based on Cochran's design was marketed to the public. By then, dishwashing detergent was improving, as was the availability of hot water in the typical American home. The KitchenAid brand was eventually purchased by Whirlpool, a household name in domestic appliances. Cochran's legacy lives on today, as dishwashers have become a fixture in the kitchens of homes and businesses all over the world.
